summary: Extends the Label Distribution Protocol (LDP) so it can signal the Maximum Transmission Unit for a Label Switched Path. This is needed for path MTU discovery as in RFC 1191 to work properly. It is experimental.

eli5.summary: A road should tell drivers how wide a truck may be. This lets a tunnel say how big a packet can be.

questions: how does mtu signalling work in mpls
why is automatic mtu discovery needed for label switched paths
subtitle: Automatic MTU discovery for MPLS tunnels

tldr.problem: MPLS Label Switched Paths lack a way to automatically signal the maximum packet size they can carry, forcing operators to configure MTU values manually.
tldr.mechanism: LDP adds a TLV (Type-Length-Value) option to Label Mapping messages, allowing each router along the path to announce the smallest MTU from its link to the next hop down the path.
tldr.outcome: Routers can compute the MTU for a complete LSP automatically and avoid sending packets that will be silently dropped because they are too large.

today: RFC 3988 is an Experimental RFC that describes an optional extension to LDP. It has not been updated or obsoleted, so operators can use it on networks that support it, though it is not widely deployed.

sections.title: Introduction to LSP MTU Discovery
sections.content:
MPLS Label Switched Paths (LSPs) form tunnels that route traffic through networks. Packets sent into an LSP must fit within the maximum transmission unit (MTU) of every link on the path, or they will be discarded. RFC 1191 describes how IP hosts discover path MTU—the smallest MTU along a route—to avoid sending oversized packets. Without MTU signalling, LSP ingress routers do not know the MTU of a path and must be configured manually, leading to operational burden and the risk of silent packet loss if the configuration is wrong.

This RFC extends the Label Distribution Protocol (LDP), which is used to set up LSPs in MPLS networks, with a new MTU TLV. Using this TLV, each router on the path reports the MTU it can support downstream, allowing the ingress router to learn the MTU of the entire path without manual configuration.
sections.eli5: A delivery truck must fit through every tunnel on its route. If nobody tells the driver the smallest tunnel, some packages get stuck inside tunnels and never arrive. MTU signalling is like calling ahead to ask how small a truck can pass through each tunnel.

sections.title: Key MTU Concepts
sections.content:
The RFC defines three related concepts. Link MTU is the size limit of a single link—the maximum packet size (including headers but not lower-layer framing) that the link can pass. Hop MTU is the MTU between two adjacent LSRs on an LSP, the minimum of the link MTU and the space needed for labels if multiple labels are stacked. LSP MTU is the MTU from a given LSR to the egress of the LSP, accounting for labels that were already in the packet when it entered the LSP.

An important detail: if an LSR adds a label to a packet, it increases the packet size by 4 bytes. The Hop MTU calculation must account for this. Egress LSRs (the end of the path) report an MTU of 65535 since they remove labels.
sections.eli5: Imagine a train going through different tunnels. Link MTU is the height of one tunnel. Hop MTU adds the height of the train itself. LSP MTU is the smallest tunnel the entire train must fit through from start to finish.

sections.title: MTU TLV Format and Signalling
sections.content:
The MTU TLV is a Type-Length-Value structure added to LDP Label Mapping messages. It contains a single 16-bit unsigned integer representing the MTU in octets. The TLV has Type 0x0601 and is marked as optional but must be forwarded by routers that do not recognize it, ensuring that older routers can interoperate with newer ones.

Each LSR along the path computes its LSP MTU for a given Forwarding Equivalence Class (FEC) and includes the MTU value in its Label Mapping to the upstream LSR. The LSP MTU is the minimum of the Hop MTU to each downstream LSR and the LSP MTU advertised by that downstream LSR. If a downstream LSR did not include an MTU TLV, it is assumed to support the full 65535 octets.
sections.eli5: Each router marks the label it sends with a number: the smallest size that still fits. Routers along the path keep choosing the smallest number they see, so the final number represents the tightest squeeze anywhere on the path.

sections.title: Using Computed LSP MTU
sections.content:
Once an ingress LSR knows the MTU of an LSP, it applies RFC 1191 path MTU discovery logic. If the DF (Don't Fragment) bit is clear, the LSR fragments IP packets to fit the LSP MTU. If the DF bit is set and a packet exceeds the LSP MTU, the LSR drops the packet and returns an ICMP Destination Unreachable message with code "fragmentation needed and DF set" and the LSP MTU as the next-hop MTU.

For non-IP payloads, the LSR MUST forward the packet if it fits the LSP MTU and SHOULD drop it otherwise. The ingress LSR MAY advertise an MTU smaller than it computed, for policy reasons, but MUST NOT advertise a larger one.
sections.eli5: Once you know the smallest tunnel, you either shrink your truck to fit, or you tell the shipper it won't fit. You can be extra cautious and use a smaller truck than the smallest tunnel allows, but you can't pretend a tunnel is bigger than it is.

sections.title: Deployment Across MPLS Variants
sections.content:
The MTU TLV applies to all forms of LSPs: regular LDP LSPs, Constraint-based LSPs created with CR-LDP, and LSPs signalled using RSVP-TE. The mechanism works even when LSPs tunnel through other LSPs: the inner LSP is treated as a link whose MTU is the outer LSP's MTU minus the 4 bytes for the outer label.

Routers that do not support MTU signalling will silently forward the MTU TLV to upstream routers. This preserves the maximum available information about path MTU, but the unsupporting router's link MTU is not propagated, so upstream routers must assume it supports the full 65535 octets. A network can therefore be deployed with a mix of supporting and non-supporting routers.
sections.eli5: Some routers know about MTU signalling, others do not. The smart routers pass along what they learn. If a dumb router sits in the middle, everyone assumes it has a huge tunnel, which is a safe assumption but might be wrong.
